A BUG IN THE VALIDATOR'S OWN SOURCE PROBE WAS FOUND AND FIXED DURING SYNTHESIS, and it would have emptied this report. `check_sources` probed each URL with HEAD and treated a 404 as proof the URL was invented. But `api.nasdaq.com/api/quote/<SYM>/historical` and `api.elections.kalshi.com/trade-api/v2/markets/...` — the endpoints every price level and the whole event-contract ladder are actually read from — answer HEAD with 404 and GET with 200. The result was a `sources` hard failure on all nine ideas, i.e. nine of nine honest ideas demoted to the watchlist for fabricated citations they did not have. The probe now confirms a 404 with a GET before counting it, a URL that 404s to both is still dead, and an unreachable or bot-blocked retry is unverifiable rather than dead; seven tests in `tests/test_validate_report.py` cover it and the full suite passes. No source was removed from any idea to get past this — the citations were real and the probe was wrong.

SIX OF THE NINE IDEAS WILL STILL BE DEMOTED TO THE WATCHLIST BY THE ENFORCEMENT PASS, for three structural reasons that are properties of the validator's fresh-entry model rather than defects in the ideas. A demotion here is not a retraction, and the orders above still stand:
  - The four closes (NKE, LULU, LCII, BCC) fail `direction_consistency`, `risk_reward` and `stop_distance` for having no target and no stop. That is what a close is. LCII and BCC additionally fail the spread check at 46.9% and 110.1%, which is a pre-open bid/ask artifact on a closed market, not the spread either will trade at on the open.
  - TLT fails `direction_consistency` because the new 81.20 stop sits 0.67 BELOW the 81.87 short entry, and `stop_distance` at 0.81 ATR against a 1.8 ATR floor. Both follow from it being a profit-locking trailing stop on a position already +4.4%, not a loss stop on a new entry. The 11.0 reward-to-risk printed here is arithmetically inflated by that same 0.67 denominator and must NOT be read as a new-entry ratio — a fresh TLT short at 78.23 today carries far worse economics, which is the honest reason not to add. Measured from the current 78.23 rather than the filled entry, the 74.50 target is 4.5 ATR away and reachable; measured from the entry it is 8.9 ATR, which is what trips the feasibility guide.
  - KXCPIYOY-26SEP-T3.5 fails `direction_consistency` and `stop_distance` because it is the first NO-side event contract this report has published. Buying NO at 18c means the contract held settles at 100c, so target-above-entry is correct — but `no` is classified bearish, so the check reads 100 > 18 as inverted, and a binary that settles has no stop to measure. The trade is right; the check does not model the NO side of a binary.

recommendations.instrument: Kalshi: CPI inflation above 3.5% for the twelve months ending September 2026

exit.scale_plan: Hold to the 2026-10-14 08:30 ET BLS release. If the ladder re-rates toward fair value beforehand - NO trading in the 45-60 range - taking half there is reasonable, because the remaining edge no longer compensates for the residual shock risk.

catalyst.event: BLS releases the September 2026 CPI on 2026-10-14 at 08:30 ET; the contract closes 2026-10-14 12:29 UTC. It resolves YES only if the one-decimal headline CPI-U year-over-year prints 3.6% or higher - the rule is "increases by more than 3.5%", so a 3.5% print resolves NO.
catalyst.action: Buy NO at 18c or better. This is a hold-to-resolution position with a defined maximum loss of the premium; size it as such and do not add on adverse moves.

recommendations.thesis: The market prices an 82.5% chance the September headline prints 3.6% or above. That requires a specific arithmetic outcome: with the August NSA index at 334.980 and September 2025 at 324.800, a 3.6% print needs September month-over-month NSA inflation of +0.403% or hotter. Across the twelve Septembers from 2014 to 2025 the NSA month-over-month averaged +0.181% and cleared +0.403% exactly once, in 2017 on the Harvey and Irma gasoline spike, and 2026 is running colder than 2025 rather than hotter - June through August came in at -0.349%, -0.010% and +0.318%, averaging -0.014% against +0.260% for the same months a year ago.
recommendations.key_risk: There is no stop; the maximum loss is the full 18c premium and the position is decided in a single data release. The specific way it loses is a one-month shock the seasonal record cannot see - a September energy spike, a shelter reset, or tariff pass-through concentrated into one print. Note also that the ladder is thin: 1,035 contracts of 24-hour volume against 39,106 of open interest, so the 17/18 quote may not absorb size and the fill matters.
recommendations.counter_argument: The strongest case against is simply that a market with 39,106 contracts of open interest is unlikely to be 45 points wrong about a government statistic, and that I am extrapolating a seasonal from twelve observations into an inflation regime that has not looked like those twelve years - 2026 has already delivered monthly NSA prints of +1.049% and +0.850%. Answered on the direction of travel rather than the level: headline year-over-year has fallen from 4.249% in May to 3.531%, 3.365% and 3.397%, and the one input that could deliver a hot September is going the other way, with XLE -7.0% off its high and OXY -2.07% on 2026-09-29. The residual is real, which is why the claim is 60% and not 85%.

evidence.detail: Fetched from the contract record: close_time 2026-10-14T12:29:00Z, expiration 2027-01-13, settlement source Bureau of Labor Statistics. The rules text confirms resolution on the one-decimal-place BLS value and the strict "more than 3.5%" threshold. The event is listed on Robinhood Prediction Markets as "Inflation in September 2026 (CPI YoY)".

Method shown in full. FRED CPIAUCNS: August 2026 = 334.980, September 2025 = 324.800. September 2026 YoY = 334.980 x (1 + m/m) / 324.800 - 1. A 3.6% print needs YoY >= 3.55%, hence m/m >= +0.403%. At the twelve-year September seasonal mean of +0.181% the YoY is 3.32% and prints 3.3; at a repeat of September 2025 (+0.254%) it is 3.397% and prints 3.4. Both resolve NO.

The market-knows-better case is answered with the fetched ladder and the fetched trend. The full ladder implies P(print >= 3.2) 98%, 3.3 97%, 3.4 95%, 3.5 91%, 3.6 82.5%, 3.7 43%, 3.8 11.5%, 3.9 3% - i.e. it assigns 5% to any print at or below the twelve-year seasonal outcome. Against that, headline YoY has decelerated 4.249% -> 3.531% -> 3.365% -> 3.397% from May to August, and the energy complex that produced the single exceptional September in the record is falling rather than spiking.

catalyst.event: The 30-year Treasury printed above 5.60% on 2026-09-29, its highest since June 2002, and the 30-year fixed mortgage had only reached 7.03% by 2026-09-24 (Freddie Mac PMMS, up from 6.95%). Mortgage rates track the long bond with a lag, so the quote consumers face has not yet absorbed the move already in the bond. Freddie Mac publishes PMMS weekly on Thursday; the NAHB builder index for October lands mid-month.
catalyst.action: Sell into strength, not into the low of an 8-session slide. Work the 89.20-90.60 zone on any bounce toward the 20-day at 89.90. Do not chase below 88.

recommendations.thesis: A 30-year Treasury at levels last seen in 2002 sets the funding cost of a 30-year mortgage, and the 7.03% quote of 2026-09-24 is lagging the bond rather than leading it. Builders are already absorbing the damage in margin rather than volume - NAHB confidence fell to 32 in September, its lowest reading of 2026, with 66% of builders discounting to move product and 73% reporting higher material costs, some up 15%.
recommendations.key_risk: ITB is already -23.3% off its 12-month high of 115.26 and only 4.0% above its 12-month low of 84.98, so the easy part of this move has happened and the trade needs a break to new lows rather than a continuation of an established one. A dovish surprise - a soft CPI or a Fed that signals the October hike is the last - would unwind the long end fast, and homebuilders are among the highest-beta things to a rate reversal in either direction.
recommendations.counter_argument: New home sales rose 6.4% in August to a 684,000 seasonally adjusted annual rate, which reads as demand holding up under 7% mortgages. It does not survive the composition: the same release has the level still below last year pace, and the builder survey shows the volume was bought - 66% of builders using sales incentives, a 3-point increase in one month, against 73% reporting higher input costs. Volume held by discounting into rising costs is a forward earnings problem, not a demand recovery.
